subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Evaluate ∫ (a sinx + b cosx)/(sinx + cosx) dx from 0 to π/2.

mark_split.label: Apply the property with a = π/2

steps.label: Apply the property with a = π/2
steps.margin_note: One mark. State the property before using it.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π/2 − x) = cosx and cos(π/2 − x) = sinx — the two swap places.
steps.why: Stating the property first, with the given integral labelled (1), sets up the second form that will be added to it.
common_mistakes: Skipping the property statement and jumping straight to the substitution.
Mislabelling which integral is (1) and which will be (2).

steps.label: Write the second form
steps.margin_note: One more mark. sinx and cosx swap under x → π/2 − x.
steps.memory_tip: Under x → π/2 − x, every sinx becomes cosx and every cosx becomes sinx — swap them consistently everywhere.
steps.why: Every sinx becomes cosx and every cosx becomes sinx under the substitution, so the numerator's a and b swap partners while the denominator (being symmetric in sinx and cosx) is unchanged.
common_mistakes: Swapping the numerator but forgetting the denominator is unchanged (it already contains both sinx and cosx).
Swapping only one of the two terms in the numerator.

steps.label: Add and solve
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Adding (1) and (2) makes (a+b) a common factor of the whole numerator.
steps.memory_tip: a(sinx+cosx) + b(cosx+sinx) = (a+b)(sinx+cosx) — the denominator cancels completely.

lines.text: b(\cos x+\sin x)]/(\cos x+\sin x) dx

steps.why: Adding the two forms lets (a+b) factor out of the whole numerator, which then cancels exactly with the denominator sinx+cosx, leaving a plain constant to integrate.
common_mistakes: Not factoring (a+b) out correctly before cancelling with the denominator.
Forgetting the final division by 2 when isolating I from 2I.
